stem: Three balls are drawn at random without replacement from an urn containing 6 white and 4 black balls. What is the probability that at least one ball is black?

per_option_rationale.rationale: P(at least one black) = 1 - P(none black) = 1 - C(6,3)/C(10,3) = 1 - 20/120 = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6.
Computes 1 - C(6,3)/C(10,3) but uses C(10,3) = 90 (wrong: should be 120), giving 1 - 20/90 = 70/90 = 7/9, then rounds to 2/3.
Directly adds P(exactly 1 black) only = C(4,1)*C(6,2)/C(10,3) = 60/120 - but miscalculates, arriving at 11/30 while omitting the exactly-2 and exactly-3 cases.
Reads P(no black) = C(6,3)/C(10,3) = 20/120 = 1/6 but reports this complement probability as the final answer instead of subtracting from 1.

explanation: Use the complement: at least one black = 1 - (all white). P(all white) = C(6,3)/C(10,3) = 20/120 = 1/6. So P(at least one black) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6.

explanation_sections.punchline: At-least-one is fastest via complement: 1 - P(all white) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: classical probability, without-replacement draws -> combinations. Setup decision: use complement because at-least-one problems have multiple favourable sub-cases; complement (none) is a single case. Compute P(all 3 white) = C(6,3)/C(10,3) = 20/120 = 1/6. Subtract from 1.
explanation_sections.lesson: For at-least-one problems, always evaluate the complement (none of that type) and subtract from 1 - it is almost always the quickest route.
explanation_sections.timing: 35 seconds. C(10,3) = 120, C(6,3) = 20 are quick to compute. The trap is option 4 which stops at the complement value.
